claim: Mutations in UBQLN2 cause X-linked forms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) through unknown mechanisms.
source: Mutations in the ubiquitin (Ub) chaperone Ubiquilin 2 (UBQLN2) cause X-linked forms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) through unknown mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about UBQLN2 mutations.

claim: Aggregation-prone, ALS-associated mutants of UBQLN2 (UBQLN2ALS) trigger heat stress-dependent neurodegeneration in Drosophila.
source: Here, we show that aggregation-prone, ALS-associated mutants of UBQLN2 (UBQLN2ALS) trigger heat stress-dependent neurodegeneration in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: A genetic modifier screen implicated endolysosomal and axon guidance genes, including the netrin receptor, Unc-5, as key modulators of UBQLN2 toxicity.
source: A genetic modifier screen implicated endolysosomal and axon guidance genes, including the netrin receptor, Unc-5, as key modulators of UBQLN2 toxicity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic screen described in the study.

claim: Reduced gene dosage of Unc-5 or its coreceptor Dcc/frazzled diminished neurodegenerative phenotypes, including motor dysfunction, neuromuscular junction defects, and shortened lifespan, in flies expressing UBQLN2ALS alleles.
source: Reduced gene dosage of Unc-5 or its coreceptor Dcc/frazzled diminished neurodegenerative phenotypes, including motor dysfunction, neuromuscular junction defects, and shortened lifespan, in flies expressing UBQLN2ALS alleles.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Drosophila experiments.

claim: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) harboring UBQLN2ALS knockin mutations exhibited lysosomal defects.
source: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) harboring UBQLN2ALS knockin mutations exhibited lysosomal defects while inducible motor neurons (iMNs) expressing UBQLN2ALS alleles exhibited cytosolic UBQLN2 inclusions, reduced neurite complexity, and growth cone defects that were partially reversed by silencing of UNC5B and DCC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the iPSC experiments.

claim: Inducible motor neurons (iMNs) expressing UBQLN2ALS alleles exhibited cytosolic UBQLN2 inclusions.
source: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) harboring UBQLN2ALS knockin mutations exhibited lysosomal defects while inducible motor neurons (iMNs) expressing UBQLN2ALS alleles exhibited cytosolic UBQLN2 inclusions, reduced neurite complexity, and growth cone defects that were partially reversed by silencing of UNC5B and DCC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the iMN experiments.

claim: Inducible motor neurons (iMNs) expressing UBQLN2ALS alleles exhibited reduced neurite complexity.
source: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) harboring UBQLN2ALS knockin mutations exhibited lysosomal defects while inducible motor neurons (iMNs) expressing UBQLN2ALS alleles exhibited cytosolic UBQLN2 inclusions, reduced neurite complexity, and growth cone defects that were partially reversed by silencing of UNC5B and DCC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the iMN experiments.

claim: Inducible motor neurons (iMNs) expressing UBQLN2ALS alleles exhibited growth cone defects.
source: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) harboring UBQLN2ALS knockin mutations exhibited lysosomal defects while inducible motor neurons (iMNs) expressing UBQLN2ALS alleles exhibited cytosolic UBQLN2 inclusions, reduced neurite complexity, and growth cone defects that were partially reversed by silencing of UNC5B and DCC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the iMN experiments.

claim: Growth cone defects in UBQLN2ALS iMNs were partially reversed by silencing of UNC5B and DCC.
source: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) harboring UBQLN2ALS knockin mutations exhibited lysosomal defects while inducible motor neurons (iMNs) expressing UBQLN2ALS alleles exhibited cytosolic UBQLN2 inclusions, reduced neurite complexity, and growth cone defects that were partially reversed by silencing of UNC5B and DCC.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the iMN experiments with genetic manipulation.

claim: Altered growth cone dynamics are a conserved pathomechanism in UBQLN2-associated ALS/FTD.
source: The combined findings suggest that altered growth cone dynamics are a conserved pathomechanism in UBQLN2-associated ALS/FTD.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined findings in flies and human cells.

claim: Defective protein folding and proteostatic stress are common pathogenic mechanisms linking genetically and anatomically diverse neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Defective protein folding and proteostatic stress are common pathogenic mechanisms linking genetically and anatomically diverse neurodegenerative diseases (Ling et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ling et al., 2013.

claim: The steady state levels and neurotoxicity of aggregation-prone proteins are determined through a balance of protein production and protein clearance.
source: The steady state levels—and ultimately neurotoxicity—of aggregation-prone proteins are determined through a balance of protein production and protein clearance (Prahlad and Morimoto, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Prahlad and Morimoto, 2009.

claim: The convergence of aging-dependent declines in protein degradation and nuclear import with environmental stresses may push the protein balance equation toward irreversible protein aggregation that sets the stage for neurodegenerative processes.
source: The convergence of aging-dependent declines in protein degradation and nuclear import with environmental stresses may push this equation toward irreversible protein aggregation that sets the stage for neurodegenerative processes (Morimoto, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morimoto, 2008 and represents a speculative mechanism.

claim: Enhancing protein degradation capacity or reducing the aggregation potential of aggregation-prone proteins represents a promising therapeutic avenue for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and other neurodegenerative proteinopathies.
source: Thus, enhancing protein degradation capacity—or reducing the aggregation potential of aggregation-prone proteins—represents a promising therapeutic avenue for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and other neurodegenerative proteinopathies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the preceding discussion of protein homeostasis.

claim: The highly conserved ubiquilin (UBQLN) gene family fulfills diverse roles in protein folding, shuttling, and degradation.
source: The highly conserved ubiquilin (UBQLN) gene family fulfills diverse roles in protein folding, shuttling, and degradation (Zheng et al., 2020; Rothenberg and Monteiro, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zheng et al., 2020 and Rothenberg and Monteiro, 2010.

claim: All eukaryotic UBQLNs feature an amino-terminal ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain and a carboxyl-terminal ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain separated by a low complexity, methionine-rich central region harboring variable numbers of STI1-like repeats.
source: All eukaryotic UBQLNs feature an amino-terminal ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain and a carboxyl-terminal ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain separated by a low complexity, methionine-rich central region harboring variable numbers of STI1-like repeats first identified in the yeast stress-inducible 1 (Sti1) protein and later described in several distinct classes of protein chaperones (Fry et al., 2021; Zientara-Rytter and Subramani, 2019; Howe et al., 2020; Schmid et al., 2012; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing UBQLN structure.

claim: Mammals encode four ubiquilin proteins of which three (UBQLN1, UBQLN2, and UBQLN4) are widely expressed.
source: Mammals encode four ubiquilin proteins of which three (UBQLN1, UBQLN2, and UBQLN4) are widely expressed.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mammalian ubiquilins.

claim: UBQLN1 and UBQLN2 share >70% amino acid identity and are presumed to function in semi-redundant fashion.
source: UBQLN1 and UBQLN2 share >70% amino acid identity and are presumed to function in semi-redundant fashion, whereas UBQLN4 is a more distantly related paralog.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about UBQLN1 and UBQLN2 relationship.

claim: UBQLN4 is a more distantly related paralog to UBQLN1 and UBQLN2.
source: UBQLN1 and UBQLN2 share >70% amino acid identity and are presumed to function in semi-redundant fashion, whereas UBQLN4 is a more distantly related paralog.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about UBQLN4.

claim: A generic model for UBQLN function holds that the UBA domain engages ubiquitylated substrate while the UBL domain engages the proteasome, leading to substrate degradation.
source: Although specific functions of individual ubiquilins in mammals are largely unknown, a generic model for UBQLN function holds that the UBA domain engages ubiquitylated substrate while the UBL domain engages the proteasome, leading to substrate degradation (Itakura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Itakura et al., 2016.

claim: STI1-like repeats form a hydrophobic groove that is thought to engage hydrophobic regions of client proteins.
source: STI1-like repeats form a hydrophobic groove that is thought to engage hydrophobic regions of client proteins (Fry et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fry et al., 2021.

claim: UBQLN deficiency leads to defects in autophagy and ER-associated protein degradation.
source: It has been reported that UBQLN deficiency (Df) leads to defects in autophagy and ER-associated protein degradation (Rothenberg et al., 2010; Lim et al., 2009; N'Diaye et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The central methionine-rich domain of UBQLN has been shown to bind transmembrane domains of mitochondrial proteins, which appears central to their UBQLN-dependent triage and degradation.
source: The central methionine-rich domain has been shown to bind transmembrane domains of mitochondrial proteins, which appears central to their UBQLN-dependent triage and degradation (Itakura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Itakura et al., 2016.

claim: Dominant mutations in UBQLN2 cause X-linked ALS/frontotemporal dementia (FTD).
source: Interest in ubiquilin function was greatly stimulated by the discovery that dominant mutations in UBQLN2 cause X-linked ALS/frontotemporal dementia (FTD) (Deng et al., 2011; Gellera et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deng et al., 2011 and Gellera et al., 2013.

claim: Most ALS-associated mutations in UBQLN2 are clustered within a 42-amino acid proline-rich repeat (PRR) that is unique to UBQLN2.
source: Most ALS-associated mutations in UBQLN2 are clustered within 42-amino acid proline-rich repeat (PRR) that is unique to UBQLN2 (Deng et al., 2011) however, disease-linked mutations outside this region have also been described (Synofzik et al., 2012; Daoud et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deng et al., 2011, Synofzik et al., 2012, and Daoud et al., 2012.

claim: Disease-linked mutations in UBQLN2 outside the PRR region have been described.
source: Most ALS-associated mutations in UBQLN2 are clustered within 42-amino acid proline-rich repeat (PRR) that is unique to UBQLN2 (Deng et al., 2011) however, disease-linked mutations outside this region have also been described (Synofzik et al., 2012; Daoud et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Synofzik et al., 2012 and Daoud et al., 2012.

claim: UBQLN2-mutant patients exhibit a range of phenotypes that includes FTD, ALS, and spastic paraplegia.
source: In addition, UBQLN2-mutant patients exhibit a range of phenotypes that includes FTD, ALS, and spastic paraplegia (Gkazi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gkazi et al., 2019.

claim: Ubiquilin-positive aggregates are a near universal occurrence in TDP-43-positive ALS, as well as ALS linked to C9ORF72 expansions (C9-ALS).
source: Interestingly, ubiquilin-positive aggregates are a near universal occurrence in TDP-43-positive ALS, as well as ALS linked to C9ORF72 expansions (C9-ALS) (Brettschneider et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brettschneider et al., 2012.

claim: Ubiquilin pathology may contribute to the molecular pathogenesis of ALS even in the absence of UBQLN2 gene mutations.
source: These correlative findings suggest that ubiquilin pathology may contribute to the molecular pathogenesis of ALS even in the absence of UBQLN2 gene mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of ubiquilin aggregates in non-UBQLN2 mutant ALS.

claim: Transgenic or virus-directed expression of UBQLN2ALS mutants in rodents recapitulates protein UBQLN2 inclusions seen in ALS/FTD patients.
source: Transgenic or virus-directed expression of UBQLN2ALS mutants in rodents recapitulates protein UBQLN2 inclusions seen in ALS/FTD patients and elicits variable phenotypic abnormalities ranging to mild gait and memory defects to neuronal loss, paralysis, and early death (Gorrie et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2016; Le et al., 2016; Sharkey et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to rodent studies.

claim: Transgenic or virus-directed expression of UBQLN2ALS mutants in rodents elicits variable phenotypic abnormalities ranging from mild gait and memory defects to neuronal loss, paralysis, and early death.
source: Transgenic or virus-directed expression of UBQLN2ALS mutants in rodents recapitulates protein UBQLN2 inclusions seen in ALS/FTD patients and elicits variable phenotypic abnormalities ranging to mild gait and memory defects to neuronal loss, paralysis, and early death (Gorrie et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2016; Le et al., 2016; Sharkey et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to rodent studies.

claim: Coexpression of UBQLN2P497H and an ALS-associated TDP-43 allele under control of the neurofilament heavy gene promoter caused severe motor neuron loss and muscle wasting.
source: Coexpression of UBQLN2P497H and an ALS-associated TDP-43 allele under control of the neurofilament heavy gene promoter caused severe motor neuron loss and muscle wasting (Picher-Martel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Picher-Martel et al., 2019.

claim: Brain-directed expression of wild-type UBQLN2 caused toxicity phenotypes.
source: Brain-directed expression of wild-type UBQLN2 also caused toxicity phenotypes (Huang et al., 2016; Le et al., 2016; Sharkey et al., 2020), potentially due to disruptions in Ub homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2016, Le et al., 2016, and Sharkey et al., 2020.

claim: Brain-directed expression of wild-type UBQLN2 toxicity is potentially due to disruptions in Ub homeostasis.
source: Brain-directed expression of wild-type UBQLN2 also caused toxicity phenotypes (Huang et al., 2016; Le et al., 2016; Sharkey et al., 2020), potentially due to disruptions in Ub homeostasis.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed toxicity.

claim: UBQLN2 harbors low complexity regions and undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation.
source: Finally, like many proteins implicated in ALS/FTD (Pakravan et al., 2021), UBQLN2 harbors low complexity regions and undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (Sharkey et al., 2018; Dao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sharkey et al., 2018 and Dao et al., 2018.

claim: ALS-associated mutations in the PRR may interfere with UBQLN2 liquid demixing.
source: While ALS-associated mutations in the PRR may interfere with UBQLN2 liquid demixing, the relevance to disease pathogenesis is presently unclear.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential mechanism.

claim: The relevance of UBQLN2 liquid demixing interference to disease pathogenesis is presently unclear.
source: While ALS-associated mutations in the PRR may interfere with UBQLN2 liquid demixing, the relevance to disease pathogenesis is presently unclear.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about the mechanism.

claim: Expression of ALS-associated UBQLN2 mutants caused mutation-dependent neurotoxicity in Drosophila.
source: In previous work, we reported that expression of ALS-associated UBQLN2 mutants caused mutation-dependent neurotoxicity in Drosophila (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Endolysosomal dysfunction and axon guidance defects are phenotypic drivers of neurodegeneration in UBQLN2-associated ALS/FTD.
source: Our findings suggest that endolysosomal dysfunction and axon guidance defects are phenotypic drivers of neurodegeneration in UBQLN2-associated ALS/FTD.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the combined findings.

claim: Homozygous expression of single-copy human UBQLN2ALS alleles caused mild eye toxicity when expressed under control of an eye-specific GMR driver at 22°C.
source: We previously reported that homozygous expression of single-copy human UBQLN2ALS alleles caused mild eye toxicity when expressed under control of an eye-specific GMR driver at 22°C (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: UBQLN2-associated phenotypes may be worsened by heat stress.
source: Reasoning that UBQLN2-associated phenotypes may be worsened by heat stress (HS), we compared eye morphologies between flies expressing UBQLN2WT, a clinical UBQLN2P497H allele, and a highly aggregation-prone UBQLN24XALS mutant that harbors four different clinical mutations (P497H, P506T, P509S, and P525S, Figure 1A; Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is the reasoning behind the experimental design.

claim: None of the UBQLN2 transgenes caused an overt external eye phenotype when expressed from a hemizygous GMR>UBQLN2 Chr2 locus at 22°C.
source: None of the UBQLN2 transgenes caused an overt external eye phenotype when expressed from a hemizygous GMR>UBQLN2 Chr2 locus at 22°C (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies exhibited a moderately severe rough eye (RE) phenotype characterized by eye depigmentation and loss of ommatidial facets in both male and female flies at 29°C.
source: By contrast, GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies—but not GMR>UBQLN2WT or GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies—exhibited a moderately severe rough eye (RE) phenotype that was characterized by eye depigmentation and loss of ommatidial facets in both male and female flies (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: UBQLN24XALS was significantly less soluble than UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H at both 22°C and 29°C.
source: As expected, UBQLN24XALS was significantly less soluble than UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H at both 22°C and 29°C; however, the relative proportion of insoluble UBQLN24XALS was comparable at both temperatures, suggesting that increased aggregation of UBQLN24XALS cannot wholly account for its enhanced toxicity at 29°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The relative proportion of insoluble UBQLN24XALS was comparable at both 22°C and 29°C.
source: As expected, UBQLN24XALS was significantly less soluble than UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H at both 22°C and 29°C; however, the relative proportion of insoluble UBQLN24XALS was comparable at both temperatures, suggesting that increased aggregation of UBQLN24XALS cannot wholly account for its enhanced toxicity at 29°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Increased aggregation of UBQLN24XALS cannot wholly account for its enhanced toxicity at 29°C.
source: As expected, UBQLN24XALS was significantly less soluble than UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H at both 22°C and 29°C; however, the relative proportion of insoluble UBQLN24XALS was comparable at both temperatures, suggesting that increased aggregation of UBQLN24XALS cannot wholly account for its enhanced toxicity at 29°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the solubility data.

claim: The average number of peptide spectral matches for hUBQLN2 was comparable between GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 22°C and 29°C.
source: The average number of peptide spectral matches for hUBQLN2 was comparable between GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 22°C and 29°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: hUBQLN2-unique peptides were ~6-fold more abundant than dUbqln peptides in both GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS heads.
source: hUBQLN2-unique peptides were ~6-fold more abundant than dUbqln peptides in both GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS heads, providing a lower limit of hUBQLN2 overexpression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Absolute numbers of hUBQLN2 peptides were higher in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 29°C versus 22°C.
source: As expected, given the heat inducibility of UAS, absolute numbers of hUBQLN2 peptides were higher in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 29°C versus 22°C; however, the difference was not statistically significant across three replicates.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data.

claim: The difference in hUBQLN2 peptide abundance between 29°C and 22°C was not statistically significant across three replicates.
source: As expected, given the heat inducibility of UAS, absolute numbers of hUBQLN2 peptides were higher in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 29°C versus 22°C; however, the difference was not statistically significant across three replicates.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of mass spectrometry data.

claim: Each of the three GMR>UBQLN2 lines exhibited hundreds of gene expression changes relative to GMR-Gal4 controls.
source: Each of the three GMR>UBQLN2 lines exhibited hundreds of gene expression changes relative to GMR-Gal4 controls, suggesting that UBQLN2 overexpression has a substantial impact on cellular regulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: UBQLN2 overexpression has a substantial impact on cellular regulation.
source: Each of the three GMR>UBQLN2 lines exhibited hundreds of gene expression changes relative to GMR-Gal4 controls, suggesting that UBQLN2 overexpression has a substantial impact on cellular regulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-Seq data.

claim: GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies exhibited a distinct RNA-Seq gene expression signature relative to GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies.
source: Consistent with their more severe eye phenotype, GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies exhibited a distinct RNA-Seq gene expression signature relative to GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies, which clustered together in principle component analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 629 genes were uniquely changed in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies versus GMR>UBQLN2WT, GMR>UBQLN2P497H, and GMR-Gal4 controls at 29°C.
source: Using an FDR of <0.05, 629 genes were uniquely changed in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies versus GMR>UBQLN2WT, GMR>UBQLN2P497H, and GMR-Gal4 controls at 29°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 402 genes were upregulated in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies.
source: Of these, 402 genes were upregulated and 227 genes were downregulated in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E, Supplementary Dataset 1 and 2, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E.

claim: 227 genes were downregulated in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies.
source: Of these, 402 genes were upregulated and 227 genes were downregulated in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E, Supplementary Dataset 1 and 2, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E.

claim: mRNAs involved in eye development and phototransduction, including inaC, ninaE, and Rh3, were broadly downregulated in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies, likely reflecting degenerative cell loss.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis revealed that mRNAs involved in eye development and phototransduction, including inaC, ninaE, and Rh3, were broadly downregulated in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies, likely reflecting degenerative cell loss (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E, Supplementary Dataset 2).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: Upregulated GO terms in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies included response to biotic stimulus, which includes Drosophila innate immunity genes such as Dro, AttB, AttC, and Listericin.
source: Upregulated GO terms included response to biotic stimulus, which includes Drosophila innate immunity genes such as Dro, AttB, AttC, and Listericin, and response to UV light, which includes the small heat-shock protein-encoding genes Hsp23, Hsp26, and Hsp27 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E, Supplementary Dataset 1).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: Upregulated GO terms in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies included response to UV light, which includes the small heat-shock protein-encoding genes Hsp23, Hsp26, and Hsp27.
source: Upregulated GO terms included response to biotic stimulus, which includes Drosophila innate immunity genes such as Dro, AttB, AttC, and Listericin, and response to UV light, which includes the small heat-shock protein-encoding genes Hsp23, Hsp26, and Hsp27 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E, Supplementary Dataset 1).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: Upregulation of HSPs may be driven by UBQLN24XALS misfolding.
source: Upregulation of HSPs may be driven by UBQLN24XALS misfolding.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed upregulation of HSPs.

claim: Only 64 genes were differentially expressed between GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies.
source: In contrast to the profound differences between GMR>UBQLN24XALS and GMR>UBQLN2WT flies, only 64 genes were differentially expressed between GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies, which is consistent with their qualitatively similar eye phenotypes.
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data.

claim: 28 differentially expressed genes were common to GMR>UBQLN24XALS and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies relative to GMR>UBQLN2WT flies.
source: Finally, 28 differentially expressed genes were common to GMR>UBQLN24XALS and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies relative to GMR>UBQLN2WT flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The strong eye phenotype of GMR>UBQLN24XALS is accompanied by robust changes in gene expression.
source: Overall, these findings reveal that the strong eye phenotype of GMR>UBQLN24XALS is accompanied by robust changes in gene expression.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the RNA-Seq data.

claim: A Bloomington Df library of 194 lines spanning 85% of chromosome 2 was screened for UBQLN2ALS modifiers.
source: To this end, we screened a Bloomington Df library of 194 lines spanning 85% of chromosome 2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the genetic screen methodology.

claim: The UBQLN24XALS screen identified seven suppressors.
source: The UBQLN24XALS screen identified seven suppressors, three of which overlapped a common genomic interval, and 23 enhancers, including 15 lethal enhancers (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic screen shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The UBQLN24XALS screen identified 23 enhancers, including 15 lethal enhancers.
source: The UBQLN24XALS screen identified seven suppressors, three of which overlapped a common genomic interval, and 23 enhancers, including 15 lethal enhancers (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic screen shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The UBQLN2P497H screen identified six enhancers, two of which were also identified in the UBQLN24XALS screen.
source: The UBQLN2P497H screen identified six enhancers, two of which were also identified in the UBQLN24XALS screen (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic screen shown in Figure 2D.

claim: All Dfs that enhanced the GMR>UBQLN2P497H eye phenotype also caused enhanced eye phenotypes in GMR>UBQLN2WT flies.
source: Notably, all Dfs that enhanced the GMR>UBQLN2P497H eye phenotype also caused enhanced eye phenotypes in GMR>UBQLN2WT flies.
evidence: This is an observation from the genetic screen.

claim: Rab5 knockdown phenocopied the hyperpigmented phenotype seen in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies crossed to BSC37 at 29°C.
source: In support of a role for Rab5 as a UBQLN2 modifier gene, Rab5 knockdown phenocopied the hyperpigmented phenotype seen in GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies crossed to BSC37 at 29°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Rab5 knockdown caused a hyperpigmented eye phenotype in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies.
source: Rab5 knockdown also caused a hyperpigmented eye phenotype in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), indicating Rab5 is a mutation-independent UBQLN2 enhancer.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Rab5 is a mutation-independent UBQLN2 enhancer.
source: Rab5 knockdown also caused a hyperpigmented eye phenotype in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), indicating Rab5 is a mutation-independent UBQLN2 enhancer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Rab5 knockdown affects all UBQLN2 variants.

claim: GMR>UBQLN24XALS/shRab5 flies reared at 22°C failed to exhibit eye patches.
source: Interestingly, while Rab5 knockdown also caused hyperpigmented eye patches in GMR>UBQLN2WT, and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies reared at 22°C, GMR>UBQLN24XALS/shRab5 flies reared at 22°C failed to exhibit eye patches (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: UBQLN24XALS phenotypes are heat stress dependent.
source: This finding supports the idea that UBQLN24XALS phenotypes are HS dependent and is consistent with an earlier study showing stronger eye phenotypes in GMR>UBQLN2WT and GMR>UBQLN2P497H flies relative to GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies at 22°C (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the temperature-dependent phenotypes and supported by a citation.

claim: Overexpression of GFP-Rab5 partially rescued the eye phenotype of GMR>UBQLN2WT, GMR>UBQLN2P497H, and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 29°C.
source: Finally, we showed that overexpression of GFP-Rab5 partially rescued the eye phenotype of GMR>UBQLN2WT, GMR>UBQLN2P497H, and GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies reared at 29°C (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Rab5 knockdown or overexpression did not affect UBQLN2 expression.
source: Rab5 knockdown or overexpression did not affect UBQLN2 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E, G, H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E, G, H.

claim: Rab5 is a general modulator of UBQLN2 toxicity.
source: The combined findings suggest that Rab5 is a general modulator of UBQLN2 toxicity and that UBQLN2 overexpression interferes with endolysosomal function in flies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Rab5 experiments.

claim: UBQLN2 overexpression interferes with endolysosomal function in flies.
source: The combined findings suggest that Rab5 is a general modulator of UBQLN2 toxicity and that UBQLN2 overexpression interferes with endolysosomal function in flies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Rab5 experiments.

claim: lilli encodes a transcriptional elongation factor that is orthologous to mammalian AF4/FMR2 (fragile X mental retardation 2).
source: Within this overlap we identified lilliputian (lilli) as a gene of interest. lilli encodes a transcriptional elongation factor that is orthologous to mammalian AF4/FMR2 (fragile X mental retardation 2) (Wittwer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wittwer et al., 2001.

claim: lilli mutations were shown to suppress toxicity of TDP-43 and C9ORF72-derived dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) in Drosophila.
source: Interestingly, lilli mutations were recently shown to suppress toxicity of TDP-43 and C9ORF72-derived dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) in Drosophila (Chung et al., 2018; Yuva-Aydemir et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chung et al., 2018 and Yuva-Aydemir et al., 2019.

claim: A lilliA17-2 LOF allele diminished UBQLN24XALS-mediated eye toxicity to a similar extent as lilli-spanning Dfs.
source: In support of lilli as a UBQLN24XALS suppressor, a lilliA17-2 LOF allele diminished UBQLN24XALS-mediated eye toxicity to a similar extent as lilli-spanning Dfs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: lilli may be of interest as a general suppressor of toxicity arising from misexpression of neurodegeneration-associated genes in Drosophila.
source: Thus, lilli may be of interest as a general suppressor of toxicity arising from misexpression of neurodegeneration-associated genes in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation that lilli suppresses multiple ALS-related proteins.

claim: Unc-5 encodes a transmembrane dependence receptor that mediates axonal repulsion and apoptosis suppression in response to secreted netrin ligands.
source: The region of overlap between ED2426 and BSC346 contains Unc-5, which encodes a transmembrane dependence receptor that mediates axonal repulsion and apoptosis suppression in response to secreted netrin ligands (Boyer and Gupton, 2018; Labrador et al., 2005; Keleman and Dickson, 2001; Llambi et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2009; Ahn et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing Unc-5 function.

claim: Two Unc-5 LOF alleles and three different RNAi lines diminished the RE phenotype of GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies without affecting UBQLN2 expression.
source: In support of a genetic interaction between Unc-5 and UBQLN24XALS, two Unc-5 LOF alleles (Labrador et al., 2005), and three different RNAi lines diminished the RE phenotype of GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies without affecting UBQLN2 expression (Figure 3C, D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C, D and E.

claim: Unc-5 knockdown had no effect on the RE phenotype caused by the expression of ALS-associated FUS alleles.
source: By contrast, Unc-5 knockdown had no effect on the RE phenotype caused by the expression of ALS-associated FUS alleles that cause severe degenerative phenotypes in Drosophila (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Lanson et al., 2011; Kwiatkowski et al., 2009; Vance et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claim: Genetic interaction with Unc-5 may be specific to UBQLN2 versus other ectopically expressed ALS-associated proteins in Drosophila.
source: This suggests that genetic interaction with Unc-5 may be specific to UBQLN2 versus other ectopically expressed ALS-associated proteins in Drosophila.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of the Unc-5 effect.

claim: fra encodes the fly ortholog of mammalian deleted in colon carcinoma (DCC).
source: The repulsive activity of Unc-5 on axon guidance is antagonized by frazzled (fra), which encodes the fly ortholog of mammalian deleted in colon carcinoma (DCC) (Chan et al., 1996; Keino-Masu et al., 1996; Kolodziej et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chan et al., 1996, Keino-Masu et al., 1996, and Kolodziej et al., 1996.

claim: fra silencing rescued the UBQLN24XALS eye phenotype to a similar extent as Unc-5 knockdown.
source: fra silencing by two different RNAi lines rescued the UBQLN24XALS eye phenotype to a similar extent as Unc-5 knockdown (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Signaling through Unc-5/Frazzled potentiates UBQLN24XALS toxicity in the Drosophila compound eye.
source: The combined findings suggest that signaling through Unc-5/Frazzled potentiates UBQLN24XALS toxicity in the Drosophila compound eye.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction data.

claim: The moderate climbing defect of D42>UBQLN24XALS flies relative to D42-Gal4 flies was partially reversed by an shUnc-5 (TRiP) allele in both male and female flies.
source: The moderate climbing defect of D42>UBQLN24XALS flies relative to D42-Gal4 flies was partially reversed by an shUnc-5 (TRiP) allele in both male and female flies, while a second Unc-5 shRNA line (KK) rescued climbing in male but not female flies (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A second Unc-5 shRNA line (KK) rescued climbing in male but not female D42>UBQLN24XALS flies.
source: The moderate climbing defect of D42>UBQLN24XALS flies relative to D42-Gal4 flies was partially reversed by an shUnc-5 (TRiP) allele in both male and female flies, while a second Unc-5 shRNA line (KK) rescued climbing in male but not female flies (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: D42>UBQLN24XALS flies exhibited neuromuscular junction (NMJ) abnormalities, including increased numbers of satellite boutons and reduced numbers of mature boutons.
source: Consistent with their climbing defects, D42>UBQLN24XALS flies exhibited neuromuscular junction (NMJ) abnormalities, including increased numbers of satellite boutons and reduced numbers of mature boutons.
evidence: This is based on NMJ morphology analysis.

claim: NMJ abnormalities in D42>UBQLN24XALS flies were corrected by Unc-5 silencing.
source: Both phenotypes were corrected by Unc-5 silencing (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Elav>UBQLN24XALS/shUnc-5 flies showed a significant increase in lifespan relative to Elav>UBQLN24XALS flies crossed to shLuci, with the effect being most pronounced in female flies.
source: Elav>UBQLN24XALS/shUnc-5 flies showed a significant increase in lifespan relative to Elav>UBQLN24XALS flies crossed to shLuci, with the effect being most pronounced in female flies (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Unc-5 knockdown modestly increased the lifespan of Elav-Gal4 male flies relative to Elav-Gal4/shLuci flies.
source: Unc-5 knockdown also modestly increased the lifespan of Elav-Gal4 male flies relative to Elav-Gal4/shLuci flies while having no impact on lifespan of Elav-Gal4 female flies (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Unc-5 knockdown had no impact on lifespan of Elav-Gal4 female flies.
source: Unc-5 knockdown also modestly increased the lifespan of Elav-Gal4 male flies relative to Elav-Gal4/shLuci flies while having no impact on lifespan of Elav-Gal4 female flies (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Aberrant Unc-5 signaling contributes to neuronal phenotypes in UBQLN24XALS flies.
source: Altogether, these experiments suggest that aberrant Unc-5 signaling contributes to neuronal phenotypes in UBQLN24XALS flies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined Unc-5 experiments.

claim: The overlapping genetic interval spanned by the UBQLN24XALS suppressors Exel6038 and r10 contains beat-1b and beat-1c, two members of the beaten path (beat) family of axon guidance genes.
source: Interestingly, the overlapping genetic interval spanned by the UBQLN24XALS suppressors Exel6038 and r10 contains beat-1b and beat-1c, two members of the beaten path (beat) family of axon guidance genes (Figure 5A–C; Vactor et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by genetic mapping data shown in Figure 5A–C and a citation.

claim: Neuronally expressed Beat proteins regulate motor axon guidance and defasciculation in response to Sidestep (Side) ligands expressed on target substrates.
source: Neuronally expressed Beat proteins regulate motor axon guidance and defasciculation in response to Sidestep (Side) ligands expressed on target substrates (Fambrough and Goodman, 1996; Sink et al., 2001; Siebert et al., 2009; de Jong et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing Beat protein function.

claim: UBQLN24XALS flies crossed to a Beat-1b shRNA line exhibited less severe eye degeneration than UBQLN24XALS flies expressing shRNAs targeting luciferase, mCherry, or beat-1c.
source: UBQLN24XALS flies crossed to a Beat-1b shRNA line exhibited less severe eye degeneration than UBQLN24XALS flies expressing shRNAs targeting luciferase, mCherry, or beat-1c (Figure 5D, E and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D, E and F.

claim: GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies heterozygous for a p-element insertion in the beat-1b ORF exhibited improved eye phenotype relative to control GMR>UBQLN24XALS controls.
source: GMR>UBQLN24XALS flies heterozygous for a p-element insertion in the beat-1b ORF also exhibited improved eye phenotype relative to control GMR>UBQLN24XALS controls (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Beat-1b signaling contributes to UBQLN2 toxicity.
source: These findings support the idea that Beat-1b signaling contributes to UBQLN2 toxicity and further implicate axonal guidance defects as a contributing pathomechanism to UBQLN2-associated neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Beat-1b experiments.

claim: Axonal guidance defects are a contributing pathomechanism to UBQLN2-associated neurodegeneration.
source: These findings support the idea that Beat-1b signaling contributes to UBQLN2 toxicity and further implicate axonal guidance defects as a contributing pathomechanism to UBQLN2-associated neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the identification of multiple axon guidance genes as modifiers.

claim: CRISPR/CAS9 was employed to introduce ALS-associated mutations into the X-linked UBQLN2 gene in neonatal male induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs).
source: We employed CRISPR/CAS9 to introduce ALS-associated mutations into the X-linked UBQLN2 gene in neonatal male induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) (WC031i-5907-6, see Materials and methods, and Du et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the methodology for generating iPSC lines.

claim: A UBQLN22XALS allele harboring clinical P497H and P525S mutations was serendipitously derived.
source: During the course of this work, we serendipitously derived an UBQLN2 allele harboring clinical P497H and P525S mutations (termed UBQLN22XALS) as well as a UBQLN2I498X allele that truncated the UBQLN2 ORF at codon 498 within the PRR.
evidence: This describes the generation of iPSC lines.

claim: A UBQLN2I498X allele that truncated the UBQLN2 ORF at codon 498 within the PRR was derived.
source: During the course of this work, we serendipitously derived an UBQLN2 allele harboring clinical P497H and P525S mutations (termed UBQLN22XALS) as well as a UBQLN2I498X allele that truncated the UBQLN2 ORF at codon 498 within the PRR.
evidence: This describes the generation of iPSC lines.

claim: The expression and RIPA solubility of UBQLN2P497H, UBQLN22XALS, and UBQLN24XALS were comparable to UBQLN2WT in undifferentiated iPSCs.
source: The expression and RIPA solubility of UBQLN2P497H, UBQLN22XALS, and UBQLN24XALS were comparable to UBQLN2WT in undifferentiated iPSCs, while UBQLN2I498X could not be detected by Western blotting suggesting it is a null allele (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: UBQLN2I498X could not be detected by Western blotting suggesting it is a null allele.
source: The expression and RIPA solubility of UBQLN2P497H, UBQLN22XALS, and UBQLN24XALS were comparable to UBQLN2WT in undifferentiated iPSCs, while UBQLN2I498X could not be detected by Western blotting suggesting it is a null allele (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cytologic UBQLN2P497H or UBQLN24XALS aggregates were not detected in immunostaining experiments in undifferentiated iPSCs.
source: We also failed to detect cytologic UBQLN2P497H, or UBQLN24XALS aggregates in immunostaining experiments, indicating that endogenous ALS mutations are insufficient to promote UBQLN2 aggregation in undifferentiated iPSCs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Endogenous ALS mutations are insufficient to promote UBQLN2 aggregation in undifferentiated iPSCs.
source: We also failed to detect cytologic UBQLN2P497H, or UBQLN24XALS aggregates in immunostaining experiments, indicating that endogenous ALS mutations are insufficient to promote UBQLN2 aggregation in undifferentiated iPSCs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunostaining data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: UBQLN2I498X iPSCs exhibited very weak immunoreactivity with UBQLN2 antibodies.
source: As expected, UBQLN2I498X iPSCs exhibited very weak immunoreactivity with UBQLN2 antibodies.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data.

claim: The 4XALS mutation increased the chymotrypsin sensitivity of purified UBQLN2, likely due to defective folding of the PRR.
source: Previous work demonstrated that the 4XALS mutation increased the chymotrypsin sensitivity of purified UBQLN2, likely due to defective folding of the PRR (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: UBQLN24XALS exhibited a unique chymotryptic fragmentation pattern relative to UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H, suggesting that endogenous UBQLN24XALS is misfolded.
source: As shown in Figure 6C, UBQLN24XALS exhibited a unique chymotryptic fragmentation pattern relative to UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H, suggesting that endogenous UBQLN24XALS is misfolded.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and represents an inference based on the fragmentation pattern.

claim: BafA1 decreased the solubility of both wild-type and mutant UBQLN2 proteins, with the effect being most pronounced for UBQLN24XALS.
source: While MG132 had no effect (not shown), BafA1 decreased the solubility of both wild-type and mutant UBQLN2 proteins, with the effect being most pronounced for UBQLN24XALS (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The solubility of UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H recovered following BafA1 washout.
source: In addition, while the solubility of UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H recovered following BafA1 washout, the fraction of insoluble UBQLN24XALS remained elevated (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: The fraction of insoluble UBQLN24XALS remained elevated following BafA1 washout.
source: In addition, while the solubility of UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H recovered following BafA1 washout, the fraction of insoluble UBQLN24XALS remained elevated (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: The relative abundance of lipidated and non-lipidated forms of LC3 were comparable between UBQLN2WT, UBQLN2P497H, and UBQLN24XALS, and UBQLN2I498X iPSCs, suggesting similar levels of autophagic flux.
source: Finally, the relative abundance of lipidated and non-lipidated forms of LC3 were comparable between UBQLN2WT, UBQLN2P497H, and UBQLN24XALS, and UBQLN2I498X iPSCs, suggesting similar levels of autophagic flux (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D and represents an inference based on LC3 levels.

claim: UBQLN2WT, UBQLN2P497H, and UBQLN24XALS partially localized with the lysosomal marker LAMP1 in BafA1-treated iPSCs.
source: UBQLN2WT, UBQLN2P497H, and UBQLN24XALS partially localized with the lysosomal marker LAMP1 in BafA1-treated iPSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: UBQLN2 punctae did not significantly overlap with Rab5-positive endosomes.
source: By contrast, UBQLN2 punctae did not significantly overlap with Rab5-positive endosomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both the abundance and average size of lysosomes were significantly elevated in UBQLN2P497H and UBQLN24XALS iPSCs, relative to UBQLN2WT or UBQLN2I498X iPSCs.
source: Both the abundance and average size of lysosomes were significantly elevated in UBQLN2P497H and UBQLN24XALS iPSCs, relative to UBQLN2WT or UBQLN2I498X iPSCs, which exhibited qualitatively similar LysoTracker staining patterns (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The frequency of lysosomes greater than 5 μm and 10 μm was significantly elevated in UBQLN24XALS iPSCs versus UBQLN2P497H iPSCs.
source: In particular, the frequency of lysosomes greater than 5 μm and 10 μm was significantly elevated in UBQLN24XALS iPSCs versus UBQLN2P497H iPSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Endolysosomal defects exist in UBQLN2ALS iPSCs.
source: These findings support the existence of endolysosomal defects in UBQLN2ALS iPSCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lysosomal data.

claim: UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H showed largely diffuse localization patterns in iMNs.
source: UBQLN2WT, UBQLN2P497H showed largely diffuse localization patterns, whereas UBQLN24XALS formed discrete aggregates distributed throughout iMN cell bodies and axons (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: UBQLN24XALS formed discrete aggregates distributed throughout iMN cell bodies and axons.
source: UBQLN2WT, UBQLN2P497H showed largely diffuse localization patterns, whereas UBQLN24XALS formed discrete aggregates distributed throughout iMN cell bodies and axons (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: UBQLN2 aggregation was observed in iMNs differentiated from an independently generated UBQLN24XALS iPSC clone (Clone 2).
source: UBQLN2 aggregation was also observed in iMNs differentiated from an independently generated UBQLN24XALS iPSC clone (Clone 2, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H were evenly distributed throughout growth cone lamellipodia and filopodia.
source: F-actin labeling with phalloidin revealed that UBQLN2WT and UBQLN2P497H were evenly distributed throughout growth cone lamellipodia and filopodia.
evidence: This is based on phalloidin staining data.

claim: Lamellipodial UBQLN24XALS staining was generally weaker, except for occasional brightly staining aggregates that were observed in ~50% of growth cones examined.
source: Lamellipodial UBQLN24XALS staining was generally weaker, except for occasional brightly staining aggregates that were observed in ~50% of growth cones examined (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The UBQLN24XALS mutation did not significantly impact the localization of DCC, which was highly enriched in filopodial spikes in iMNs of all UBQLN2 genotypes.
source: Notably, the UBQLN24XALS mutation did not significantly impact the localization of DCC, which was highly enriched in filopodial spikes in iMNs of all UBQLN2 genotypes (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: UBQLN24XALS iMNs exhibited a significant reduction in average total neurite length, primary neurite length, and neurite branch length relative to UBQLN2WT iMNs.
source: UBQLN24XALS iMNs exhibited a significant reduction in average total neurite length, primary neurite length, and neurite branch length relative to UBQLN2WT iMNs, which manifested as an increased rate of Sholl decay (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: UBQLN24XALS iMNs exhibited an increased rate of Sholl decay.
source: UBQLN24XALS iMNs exhibited a significant reduction in average total neurite length, primary neurite length, and neurite branch length relative to UBQLN2WT iMNs, which manifested as an increased rate of Sholl decay (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Neurite length and complexity were comparable between UBQLN2P497H and UBQLN2WT iMNs.
source: By contrast, neurite length and complexity were comparable between UBQLN2P497H and UBQLN2WT iMNs, indicating the clinical P497H mutation is insufficient to disrupt neurite growth dynamics (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The clinical P497H mutation is insufficient to disrupt neurite growth dynamics.
source: By contrast, neurite length and complexity were comparable between UBQLN2P497H and UBQLN2WT iMNs, indicating the clinical P497H mutation is insufficient to disrupt neurite growth dynamics (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the neurite analysis data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: BafA1 strongly increased the size and number of UBQLN24XALS aggregates while having minimal effects on UBQLN2WT or UBQLN2P497H localization.
source: BafA1 strongly increased the size and number of UBQLN24XALS aggregates while having minimal effects on UBQLN2WT or UBQLN2P497H localization.
evidence: This is based on BafA1 treatment experiments in iMNs.

claim: BafA1-induced UBQLN24XALS aggregates were observed in two different iMN clones and were strongly colocalized with the autophagy receptor, p62.
source: BafA1-induced UBQLN24XALS aggregates were observed in two different iMN clones and were strongly colocalized with the autophagy receptor, p62 (Figure 8A, B and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A, B and D.

claim: UBQLN24XALS aggregates often colocalized with, or were adjacent to, LAMP1-positive lysosomes.
source: In addition, UBQLN24XALS aggregates often colocalized with, or were adjacent to, LAMP1-positive lysosomes (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: UBQLN24XALS only weakly colocalized with endosomal Rab5 or the autophagosome marker, LC3.
source: By contrast, UBQLN24XALS only weakly colocalized with endosomal Rab5 or the autophagosome marker, LC3 (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: The autophagy pathway suppresses endogenous UBQLN24XALS aggregation in iMNs.
source: These findings suggest that the autophagy pathway suppresses endogenous UBQLN24XALS aggregation in iMNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the BafA1 experiments.

claim: Expression of UNC5B and DCC was reduced ~40–60% in their respective shRNA-transduced iPSCs relative to iPSCs transduced with an NT shRNA vector.
source: qPCR confirmed that expression of UNC5B and DCC was reduced ~40–60% in their respective shRNA-transduced iPSCs relative to iPSCs transduced with an NT shRNA vector (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: UBQLN24XALS iMNs expressing DCC shRNA showed reduced DCC immunoreactivity at filopodial spikes.
source: UBQLN24XALS iMNs expressing DCC shRNA also showed reduced DCC immunoreactivity at filopodial spikes (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both UNC5B and DCC knockdown significantly increased average total neurite length, primary neurite length, and branch length in UBQLN24XALS iMNs relative to UBQLN24XALS iMNs expressing a non-targeting (NT) control shRNA.
source: Both UNC5B and DCC knockdown significantly increased average total neurite length, primary neurite length, and branch length in UBQLN24XALS iMNs relative to UBQLN24XALS iMNs expressing a non-targeting (NT) control shRNA (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Neither UNC5B nor DCC silencing affected the size or number of UBQLN24XALS aggregates.
source: Neither UNC5B nor DCC silencing affected the size or number of UBQLN24XALS aggregates (Figure 9—figure supplement 2), suggesting they influence toxicity pathway(s) downstream of UBQLN2 aggregation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: UNC5B and DCC influence toxicity pathway(s) downstream of UBQLN2 aggregation.
source: Neither UNC5B nor DCC silencing affected the size or number of UBQLN24XALS aggregates (Figure 9—figure supplement 2), suggesting they influence toxicity pathway(s) downstream of UBQLN2 aggregation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that UNC5B/DCC silencing rescues phenotypes without affecting aggregates.

claim: UBQLN24XALS iMNs showed a high proportion of blunt-end termini versus growth cone termini, suggesting a defect in growth cone elaboration.
source: Compared to UBQLN2WT or UBQLN2P497H iMNs, UBQLN24XALS iMNs showed a high proportion of blunt-end termini versus growth cone termini, suggesting a defect in growth cone elaboration (Figure 9B and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9B and D and represents an inference based on the morphology.

claim: A preponderance of blunt-end termini was observed in UBQLN24XALS (Clone 2) iMNs, suggesting they are a specific consequence of the 4XALS mutation.
source: A preponderance of blunt-end termini was also observed in UBQLN24XALS (Clone 2) iMNs, suggesting they are a specific consequence of the 4XALS mutation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and represents an inference based on the observation in multiple clones.

claim: UBQLN24XALS iMNs expressing UNC5B or DCC shRNAs exhibited supernumerary growth cones along primary and secondary neurites and an increase in growth cone size and abundance relative to blunt-end termini.
source: By contrast, UBQLN24XALS iMNs expressing UNC5B or DCC shRNAs exhibited supernumerary growth cones along primary and secondary neurites and an increase in growth cone size and abundance relative to blunt-end termini (Figure 9C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 9C and D.

claim: Aberrant DCC-UNC5 signaling suppresses growth cone elaboration in UBQLN24XALS iMNs.
source: These findings suggest that aberrant DCC-UNC5 signaling suppresses growth cone elaboration in UBQLN24XALS iMNs and that axon guidance defects contribute to toxicity phenotypes in fly and iMN models for UBQLN2-associated ALS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments with UNC5B and DCC knockdown.

claim: Axon guidance defects contribute to toxicity phenotypes in fly and iMN models for UBQLN2-associated ALS.
source: These findings suggest that aberrant DCC-UNC5 signaling suppresses growth cone elaboration in UBQLN24XALS iMNs and that axon guidance defects contribute to toxicity phenotypes in fly and iMN models for UBQLN2-associated ALS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined findings in flies and iMNs.

claim: Endolysosomal dysfunction and axonal guidance defects are disease drivers in UBQLN2-associated ALS.
source: Our findings support roles for endolysosomal dysfunction and axonal guidance defects as disease drivers in UBQLN2-associated ALS (Figure 10).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: A genetic Df screen in Drosophila identified 35 loci (7 suppressors and 28 enhancers) that influenced toxicity of UBQLN2ALS mutants.
source: A genetic Df screen in Drosophila identified 35 loci (7 suppressors and 28 enhancers) that influenced toxicity of UBQLN2ALS mutants.
evidence: This is a summary of the genetic screen results.

claim: The enhanced toxicity of UBQLN24XALS may be due to its enhanced aggregation potential overwhelming cellular proteostasis machinery and/or accelerating disease mechanisms that are slow to manifest in neurons harboring ALS point mutations.
